title: UK Watchdog Warns AI Agents That Handle Money May Need Financial Authorisation
excerpt: The FCA's November 24 guidance says what an agent does — not what its maker calls itself — decides whether financial regulation applies, and that regulated firms keep accountability even for third-party agents.
body:
• The UK Financial Conduct Authority updated its agentic AI guidance on November 24, warning that an AI agent that initiates transactions, moves money, arranges borrowing or makes investment decisions may require FCA authorisation.
  • Calling a business a technology provider does not settle the question — the FCA says the boundary is set by Parliament and depends on what the agent actually does.
  • Regulated firms remain responsible for compliance, and senior managers remain accountable, even when the agent is built or supplied by a third party.
  • For Indian tech firms building AI agents for UK financial services, the FCA's stated next step is early engagement: it offers AI Lab support and is launching a dedicated Agentic Policy Sprint.

The UK's Financial Conduct Authority has told technology providers and social media platforms that building an AI agent capable of handling money can bring them inside financial regulation, in updated guidance published on November 24.

"Technology providers should consider carefully the activities their agents actually undertake," the FCA said, in wording reported by PYMNTS. "Just because a business describes itself as a technology provider does not mean that they do not need to be authorized by us to provide financial services in the UK. This boundary is set by Parliament."

Who is affected — exactly

The guidance is addressed to three groups: regulated financial firms, technology providers, and social media platforms developing or deploying agentic AI products in the financial services sector. It applies to products that may require FCA regulation at launch, and to products that evolve in a way that makes regulation apply later.

It does not say every AI chatbot needs a licence. The FCA's own framing is activity-based: "As AI becomes capable of moving beyond providing information to initiating transactions, moving money, arranging borrowing or making investment decisions, all at speed and scale, firms must understand which activities require authorisation and where regulatory requirements may apply."

"These products can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive in relation to their finances and data."

— Financial Conduct Authority, agentic AI guidance, November 24, 2026

What the regulator says it will do

"We have powers to intervene if we believe regulated financial services are being offered without our authorisation and will not hesitate to use them if necessary," the FCA said. It said it will assess the services firms provide through agentic products, including how they develop over time, to ensure they keep to regulatory requirements.

The FCA also set an expectation for consumer-facing products: "We expect AI providers to help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers and also bolster these with effective operational safeguards."

PYMNTS reported that Reuters noted the statement coincided with Meta's launch of its Muse AI assistant in the UK, and that Meta told Reuters: "We've engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so." The FCA did not name any company in its guidance.

What changes for regulated firms

For firms already authorised, outsourcing the technology does not outsource the accountability. "If your regulated firm develops or deploys agentic AI or relies on a third-party provider, responsibility for complying with regulatory obligations remains with you and senior managers within your firm," the FCA said. Senior managers are responsible for AI models deployed in their area of the business, whether developed in-house or by a third party.

The FCA expects firms to demonstrate that they understand the systems they use, the degree of autonomy those systems have, the risks they create, and the controls needed to manage those risks in real time and in stress situations. It also told firms to consider whether it is appropriate to accept payments instructed by an AI agent, or from a digital wallet controlled by an AI agent, and what liabilities may arise from accepting agent instructions.

What to do next

The FCA said it and other regulators welcome early engagement, and that its AI Lab provides services to support firms developing and testing new agentic services. It intends to launch a dedicated Agentic Policy Sprint for firms, policymakers and tech providers, with expressions of interest by email through the FCA page linked above. For a provider whose agent only answers questions today, the practical test in the guidance is what the agent does next: once it starts initiating transactions or arranging borrowing, authorisation becomes the question to settle before launch, not after.
